content: The phrasing of recommendations and their respective strengths was determined primarily through moderated discussions. Any disagreements were resolved collectively by the group, arriving at a mutually acceptable position. For a minority of decisions, the final wording and strength of a recommendation were decided through voting. An external review group (ERG) provided feedback on a draft version of the guidelines, including the recommendations, following comments from the Guideline Development Group (GDG) up until early November 2018. The finalized guidelines were made available as freely downloadable PDF files on December 21, 2018. The main text of the guidelines was published in print in March 2019 as part of the consolidated guidelines on drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) treatment and was translated into all official WHO languages, excluding online annexes 3–9. The evidence reviews and recommendations were also published separately in peer-reviewed journals to further disseminate the key messages. Changes to the policy guidance will be reflected in an upcoming revision of WHO’s implementation manual, the Companion Handbook to the WHO Guidelines for the Programmatic Management of Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis, planned for early 2019. WHO’s Global Tuberculosis Programme (WHO/GTB) will collaborate closely with regional and country offices, technical and funding agencies, and partners to ensure the updated guidance is widely communicated during technical meetings and training activities. WHO/GTB will continue to monitor new evidence that may impact the validity of its recommendations. Significant findings from new studies, trials, or other valid data are expected to emerge by mid-2019, at which point WHO will engage the GDG process to determine whether revisions are necessary. The first two editions of the guidelines for the programmatic management of drug-resistant TB were published in 2006 and 2008 as collaborative efforts involving multiple partners, many of whom were members of the Green Light Committee. The 2011 update adhered to WHO’s requirements for guideline development, as outlined in the Handbook for Guideline Development (2010). This process included an initial scoping exercise, systematic reviews to summarize evidence, and the application of the GRADE approach to develop recommendations. The updated guidelines focus on the detection and treatment of drug-resistant TB in resource-limited settings. Priority topics identified by WHO and external experts include case-finding (e.g., use of rapid molecular tests, investigation of contacts and high-risk groups), treatment regimens for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) in HIV-positive and HIV-negative patients, monitoring during treatment, and models of care. The guidelines exclude topics covered by other recent WHO policy documents, such as the treatment of drug-susceptible TB, use of antiretroviral agents, treatment of isoniazid-resistant TB, and TB infection control. The 2011 update was developed through a systematic process initiated in early 2009. Priority areas for inclusion were identified from those listed as outstanding in the 2008 emergency update. The previous programmatic management of drug-resistant TB (PMDT) guidelines was evaluated via a user questionnaire. Various experts, including TB practitioners, public health professionals, national TB control program staff, guideline methodologists, civil society members, and WHO staff, were invited to form the GDG to inform the update process. A second group, comprising national TB control program staff, WHO regional TB advisors, and clinical and public health experts, served as an External Review Group (ERG). The GDG provided input on selecting questions to address controversial topics or areas warranting policy or practice changes. They also selected and scored outcomes critical for decision-making on recommendations and identified data to be retrieved and synthesized during evidence reviews. By September 2009, the scope of the guidelines, formulated questions, and selection and scoring of main outcomes were finalized. Between October 2009 and May 2010, teams from leading academic centers were commissioned to review and compile the evidence. Preliminary results of the reviews were shared with GDG members before and during a meeting held at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, from October 25–27, 2010, to develop the recommendations. The GDG used the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) framework to formulate seven priority questions for the 2011 update. These questions addressed topics such as the prevalence of MDR-TB warranting rapid drug-susceptibility testing, monitoring methods during treatment, the inclusion of specific drugs in MDR-TB regimens, shorter treatment durations, and models of care. The evidence review teams assessed the evidence for each question and its outcomes through systematic literature reviews using an approved methodology. Titles, abstracts, and full texts of relevant literature were screened using key subject and text words. The search was not limited by study type or time period. Authors in the field and GDG members were contacted to identify missing or ongoing studies. Case-based data were collected from authors of published studies to analyze effects related to bacteriology and treatment regimens. Modeling work was conducted for questions on rapid drug-susceptibility testing and monitoring methods. For the question on models of care, a review of published and unpublished studies containing full economic evaluations of MDR-TB treatment was performed. GRADE evidence profiles were prepared for each question, summarizing the intervention's effect on each outcome and the quality of evidence. The quality of evidence was assessed based on study design, limitations (risk of bias), imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, publication bias, magnitude of effect, dose-response relationships, and residual confounding. Evidence quality was categorized into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. The GDG held teleconferences to discuss the evidence, results, and their implications for recommendations. A discussant from the GDG was assigned to assess the evidence for each question and complement the evidence review teams' presentations. A preparatory meeting in September 2010 reviewed interim results related to treatment regimens, duration, and rapid drug-susceptibility testing. The GDG met in Geneva from October 25–27, 2010, to develop revised recommendations. Members reviewed evidence profiles via a password-protected electronic website before the meeting. Additional files and successive guideline versions were shared with the GDG on the same platform. During the meeting, the GDG assessed GRADE evidence profiles and used standard decision tables to transition from evidence to recommendations. Each recommendation was documented to ensure uniform consideration of evidence quality, certainty about the balance of benefits versus harms, value alignment, and intervention costs compared to alternatives.
